notes.subtitle: Lakhs, Crores, Millions & Estimation

concepts.title: The Indian place-value system
concepts.text: The places from the right are: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, lakhs, ten lakhs, crores, ten crores.

concepts.title: The international system
concepts.text: Many countries group digits in threes: ones, thousands, millions, billions. Example: 65,207,040 = sixty-five million two hundred seven thousand forty.

concepts.title: Comparing and forming numbers
concepts.text: A number with more digits is larger. If two numbers have the same number of digits, compare from the left: the first place where the digits differ decides.

concepts.title: Rounding and estimation
concepts.text: To round to the nearest thousand, look at the hundreds digit. If it is 5 or more, round up; otherwise round down. 7,48,256 → 7,48,000.

method: Put commas in the correct system first.
Read each comma group with its place name.
For conversions, use 10 lakh = 1 million.
Estimate first, then calculate exactly and compare.

notes.intro: Lakhs, crores and millions appear in news, prices and populations. In this chapter you learn to read and write very large numbers, change between the Indian and the international systems, compare them, and estimate answers quickly.
before: know place values: ones, tens, hundreds, thousands

notes.subtitle: Terms, Brackets & Order of Operations

concepts.title: Order of operations
concepts.text: Calculate in this order: (1) brackets, (2) multiplication and division from left to right, (3) addition and subtraction from left to right.

concepts.title: Terms, swapping and grouping
concepts.text: Think of subtraction as adding a negative term: 12 − 5 + 14 = 12 + (−5) + 14. Then you can add the terms in any order and in any groups.

concepts.title: Removing brackets
concepts.text: A + sign before a bracket: remove the bracket and keep the signs. 20 + (8 − 3) = 20 + 8 − 3.

concepts.title: The distributive property
concepts.text: a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c, and a × (b − c) = a × b − a × c.

method: Write the expression from the story.
Mark the terms.
Do brackets, then × and ÷, then + and −.
Use the distributive property for smart calculation.

notes.intro: An arithmetic expression is a calculation written with numbers and operations, such as 200 − 4 × 35. In this chapter you learn the correct order to calculate, how to split an expression into terms, and how brackets and the distributive property make calculations easier.
before: add, subtract, multiply and divide whole numbers

glossary.meaning: Numbers joined by +, −, × or ÷, such as 13 + 2 × 6.
The single number that the expression equals.

lessons.title: Order of operations
text: Calculate in this order: (1) brackets, (2) multiplication and division from left to right, (3) addition and subtraction from left to right.

lessons.title: Terms, swapping and grouping
text: Think of subtraction as adding a negative term: 12 − 5 + 14 = 12 + (−5) + 14. Then you can add the terms in any order and in any groups.
This makes mental maths easy: 47 + 38 − 47 = (47 − 47) + 38 = 38.
points: Move a term together with its sign.

lessons.title: Removing brackets
text: A + sign before a bracket: remove the bracket and keep the signs. 20 + (8 − 3) = 20 + 8 − 3.
A − sign before a bracket: remove the bracket and change every sign inside. 25 − (10 − 4) = 25 − 10 + 4.
points: Minus before a bracket changes every sign inside.

text: a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c, and a × (b − c) = a × b − a × c.

notes.subtitle: Tenths, Hundredths & Decimal Place Value

concepts.title: Place value after the point
concepts.text: Each place to the right is one-tenth of the place before it: ones, tenths, hundredths, thousandths.

concepts.title: Comparing decimals
concepts.text: Compare the whole parts first. If they are equal, compare tenths, then hundredths, and so on.

concepts.title: Decimals on the number line
concepts.text: Divide each unit into 10 equal parts to mark tenths. 0.3 is the third mark after 0.

concepts.title: Adding and subtracting decimals
concepts.text: Write the numbers so that the decimal points are in one column. Fill empty places with zeros. Then add or subtract as with whole numbers and keep the point in the same column.

notes.subtitle: Variables, Forming & Simplifying Expressions

concepts.title: Writing expressions from words
concepts.text: Read each phrase carefully. 'more than' means add, 'less than' means subtract (in the right order), 'times' or 'twice' means multiply.

concepts.title: Finding the value
concepts.text: Replace each letter by its number and calculate with the order of operations. Write the number in brackets if it is negative.

concepts.text: Only like terms can be added or subtracted: 7m + 2m = 9m. 7m and 8 cannot be combined.

notes.subtitle: Angles at Intersections & Transversals

concepts.title: Angles at a crossing
concepts.text: When two lines cross, four angles form. Neighbouring angles make a linear pair (sum 180°). Opposite angles are vertically opposite and equal.

concepts.title: Parallel lines and a transversal
concepts.text: A transversal crossing two parallel lines makes 8 angles: 4 at each crossing, in matching positions.

concepts.title: Testing whether lines are parallel
concepts.text: The rules also work backwards. If corresponding angles are equal, or alternate angles are equal, or co-interior angles add to 180°, then the lines are parallel.

concepts.text: When angles are written with x, use the rule (equal or 180°) to form an equation and solve it.

notes.intro: When two lines cross, they make four angles with simple rules. When a third line crosses two parallel lines, eight angles appear, and they are linked in pairs. In this chapter you learn these pairs and use them to find unknown angles and to prove the angle sum of a triangle.

lessons.title: Angles at a crossing
text: When two lines cross, four angles form. Neighbouring angles make a linear pair (sum 180°). Opposite angles are vertically opposite and equal.
If one angle is 48°, the opposite angle is 48°, and the other two are 180° − 48° = 132°.

lessons.title: Parallel lines and a transversal
text: A transversal crossing two parallel lines makes 8 angles: 4 at each crossing, in matching positions.

Corresponding angles (same position at each crossing) are equal. Alternate interior angles (inside the lines, on opposite sides of the transversal, forming a 'Z') are equal. Interior angles on the same side (forming a 'C' or 'U') add to 180°.
points: F-shape: corresponding. Z-shape: alternate. C-shape: co-interior.

lessons.title: Testing whether lines are parallel
text: The rules also work backwards. If corresponding angles are equal, or alternate angles are equal, or co-interior angles add to 180°, then the lines are parallel.

mistakes: Mixing up alternate and corresponding angles.
Using 'equal' for co-interior angles (they add to 180°).
Assuming lines are parallel without being told.
Not giving reasons.
checklist: Write the reason after each angle.
Use the F, Z, C shapes.
Check that angles on a line add to 180°.
State 'l ∥ m' when you use parallel-line rules.
